phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'sea'
Short close front [i]; the first syllable carries the stress
Medial voiced velar fricative [ɣ]; between vowels Old Norse g softened to a glide, closer to the Spanish g of 'lago' than a hard stop
Short [u], alveolar trill [r], the voiced dental fricative [ð] — the soft 'th' of 'father' — and the final nominative ending -r, syllabic after the eth

pronunciation.approximation: 'SIG-urthr' — stress the first syllable, soften the middle g almost to a glide, sound the ð as the soft 'th' of 'father', and let the final -r hang as a light voiced syllable; it is the Old Norse nominative ending, not a separate vowel.

pronunciation.note: Sigurðr is Tier 1: the eth ð is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses, and the final -r preserves the Old Norse nominative ending that English drops entirely. Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Sigurðr) and Zoëga (s.v. Sigurðr) record the form as the name of the Vǫlsung hero; the name compounds sigr, 'victory', with -vǫrðr, 'guardian', yielding 'victory-guardian', and answers to the continental German Siegfried.

domains.title: Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism
domains.subtitle: The domain of Sigurðr
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Sigurðr governed victory, dragon-slaying, heroism. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

His is the northern form of the greatest heroic story the Germanic world ever told: the foster-son of a smith who reforged his father's shattered sword, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir, the wooer of the valkyrie behind the flame, and the oath-brother destroyed by the very loyalty that made him great. What the Iliad is to Greece, the Vǫlsunga cycle is to the North.

cards.name: Gramr
cards.desc: The sword Óðinn thrust into the tree Barnstokkr and only Sigmundr could draw; shattered in his last battle, reforged by Reginn for the son who would avenge him.

cards.name: Fáfnir at Gnitaheiðr
cards.desc: The brother turned dragon by greed, slain by a hero lying in a trench; from his heart-blood Sigurðr learned the speech of birds.

cards.name: The Flame-Wall
cards.desc: Through the vafrlogi on Hindarfjall rode Grani's rider to wake Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn had sunk in sleep — the oath sworn there could not survive the world of men.

cards.name: The Cursed Hoard
cards.desc: Andvari's gold, paid as weregild for Ótr and cursed at its surrender; every hand it passed through — Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, the Gjúkings — it brought to ruin.

symbols.name: Gramr
symbols.meaning: The reforged sword of Sigmundr, drawn from Barnstokkr and mended by Reginn; with it Sigurðr slew Fáfnir

symbols.name: Grani
symbols.meaning: The grey horse of Sleipnir's line who bore Sigurðr through the flame-wall and carried the dragon's gold from Gnitaheiðr

symbols.name: Andvaranautr and the hoard
symbols.meaning: The dwarf Andvari's ring and gold, taken as ransom and cursed at the taking — the engine of every death in the cycle

symbols.name: The dragon's heart-blood
symbols.meaning: Roasting Fáfnir's heart, Sigurðr tasted the blood and understood the birds — knowledge bought from the monster he killed

symbols.name: The vafrlogi flame-wall
symbols.meaning: The ring of fire around the sleeping Brynhildr, crossable only by the destined rider; crossed twice, once for love and once in betrayal

mythology.lead: Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy.

myths.title: The Reforging of Gramr
myths.text:
At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing — until Sigurðr demanded the shards of his father's sword be worked into the new steel. Reginn reforged them into Gramr, and the boy clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting on the current as though it were standing stone (Vǫlsunga saga 13–15; Reginsmál).

The blade binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the steel that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose. In the North, inheritance is not property but appointment.

myths.title: The Slaying of Fáfnir
myths.text:
Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who had killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr, and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man who would not give his name, Sigurðr dug a trench across the worm's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon warned him that the gold would be his death, and the hero answered with the northern creed: every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day (Fáfnismál; Vǫlsunga saga 18–20). Roasting the heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger, set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that the smith meant to kill him. He took Reginn's head, loaded the cursed gold onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North.

The birds that save him here will not be there at the end. The episode's point is exact: the monster's death transfers the monster's curse, and every new owner of the gold only inherits it.

myths.title: The Flame-Wall on Hindarfjall
myths.text:
Before the dragon, on Hindarfjall, Sigurðr found the vafrlogi — a wall of flame no horse would cross — and within it a hall where a warrior slept in full armor, as if dead. The sleep-thorn in her corslet marked her as a valkyrie; he drew Gramr and cut the armor from her, and she woke as Brynhildr and taught him the runes and the lore of the worlds: the healing runes, the ale-runes, the speech of victory and the speech of weddings, and the caution that shapes the whole cycle — never to swear falsely (Sigrdrífumál; Vǫlsunga saga 21–22). They plighted their troth and parted, and she prophesied what he would forget.

The flame-wall is the cycle's question about fate: it parts for the destined rider and for no one else, and the man it admits is not thereby saved from what comes after.

myths.title: The Ale of Forgetfulness
myths.text:
At the court of Gjúki's sons the queen Grímhildr brewed Sigurðr the ale of forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as if she had never been. He married Guðrún, swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, and when Gunnarr wooed Brynhildr and could not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with him and rode the fire in his friend's likeness — wooing his own forgotten beloved for another man, with a drawn sword laid between them in the bridal bed (Vǫlsunga saga 28; Guðrúnarkviða I). The deception could not hold: from a ring and a quarrel at the washing-stones Brynhildr learned what had been done, and wounded in her pride she demanded the death of the man who had ridden the flames and then married another.

The betrayal is the cycle's quiet engine: no one in it acts from malice until the ale is brewed — the draught of forgetfulness is the one weapon the curse of gold did not need to supply.

myths.title: The Death of Sigurðr
myths.text:
The brothers, bound to Sigurðr by oath, could not strike him; they incited the younger Guthormr, who had sworn nothing, and he stabbed Sigurðr as he slept. Some lays — Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Guðrún's own laments — have him slain out of doors, in the forest; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu, preserved only in a fragment around the Codex Regius lacuna, gives the death in bed and the last words. Dying, Sigurðr spoke gently to Guðrún, named the true traitors, and flung Gramr after the killers; the sword caught Guthormr in the doorway and took him too. Brynhildr laughed once at the bier, told the truth at last, and went onto the pyre to lie beside him (Sigurðarkviða en skamma; Vǫlsunga saga 31–32).

The sources disagree on the place but not on the meaning: the hoard's curse reached the man who thought himself above it, through the only door he had left open — the trust of those he called his own.

lore.syncretism: Sigurðr is the northern twin of a pan-Germanic hero. The continental tradition — preserved in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied (c. 1200), the Lied vom Hürnen Seyfrid, and the Old Norse Þiðreks saga, which repatriates German material — tells of the same dragon-fight, hoard, and betrayal under the name Siegfried, with the details reworked: the valkyrie becomes a Burgundian queen, the flame-wall drops away, and the murder moves to a forest spring. Scholars have long read the cycle's skeleton against history, seeing in Gunnarr and the fall of the Gjúkings the shadow of the Burgundian kingdom destroyed by the Huns in 437 — legend crystallized around remembered catastrophe. The dragon-slaying itself belongs to a still older inheritance: the Indo-European formula of the hero who kills the serpent, traced by Calvert Watkins through Indra and Vṛtra, Herakles and the Lernaean hydra, and Beowulf's fatal last fight. In later folklore the story lived on in the Faroese Sjúrðar kvæði ballads, still sung and danced in the islands centuries after the saga manuscripts were copied.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Norse figure has had a longer second life. William Morris retold the cycle in his epic The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs (1876), which he called the great story of the North that should be to all his race what the tale of Troy was to the Greeks. Richard Wagner made it the armature of Der Ring des Nibelungen — Siegfried and Götterdämmerung follow the Norse sources where the Nibelungenlied had softened them, restoring the valkyrie Brünnhilde to the centre. Arthur Rackham's illustrations fixed the cycle's visual grammar for a century, and J. R. R. Tolkien, who read the Eddas closely, composed his own The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún in Eddic metre. The dragonslayer persists in opera houses, novels, games, and film wherever a hero wins gold and is destroyed by it. In modern heathenry Sigurðr is honoured less as an object of cult than as the model of the heroic ethic — courage held fast inside a fate already written — and the runestones that depict him are among the tradition's most cited monuments. Restoring Sigurðr in Unicode keeps the eth and the nominative -r that the German Siegfried and the anglicized Sigurd alike have lost.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Sigurðr carries within it a norse understanding of victory under guard: sigr, the thing won, held by a vǫrðr, a watcher — as if the North already knew that every victory needs defending, and that the guard can fail. The hero who bore the name guarded the hoard, the oath, and the bride, and lost all three to a single draught of ale; the name outlived the man by eight centuries and counting. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form: the eth that softens the ending, the final -r that marks him as the subject of his own sentence.

lore.archaeology: The Sigurðr cycle is the most widely depicted heroic legend of the Viking Age. The Ramsund carving (Sö 101) in Södermanland, Sweden, shows the whole Gnitaheiðr episode in one frame — Sigurðr piercing the serpent from below, the heart roasting over the fire, the thumb in his mouth, the listening birds, the headless Reginn, and Grani laden with the gold — and the nearby Gök stone (Sö 327) quotes the same scene within a runic serpent band. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) in Uppland adds a further Swedish depiction, while across the North Sea the Manx cross-slabs, above all the Kirk Andreas cross, show Sigurðr roasting Fáfnir's heart, proof the legend travelled with Norse settlers. In Norway the carved portal of Hylestad stave church (c. 1200) narrates the cycle panel by panel, from the forging of Gramr to Reginn's death. The textual tradition is Icelandic and later: the heroic lays of the Poetic Edda survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), whose famous eight-leaf lacuna has cost us the fullest form of the Sigurðr lays — Brot af Sigurðarkviðu preserves only a fragment — while Vǫlsunga saga itself (c. 1270) survives in paper copies of the lost vellum NKS 1824 b 4to.
lore.originalScriptNote: The medieval Norse wrote Sigurðr in the Latin alphabet the Icelanders adapted for their vernacular, and it is in that script — Codex Regius, the Vǫlsunga saga manuscripts — that the name is preserved. The hero's own age wrote in the Younger Futhark, the sixteen-rune alphabet carved on the memorial stones that depict his deeds; reduced to sixteen signs, it did not even distinguish ð from þ or d from t, so the full sound of the name was never recoverable from runes alone. The restored form Sigurðr keeps both features the Latin-script manuscripts attest: the eth ð, the voiced dental fricative, and the nominative ending -r. As a registrable domain the Unicode form carries the eth that the ASCII sigurd flattens to d — the punycode encodes exactly what the saga scribes wrote.
